Assistant: That's fantastic news, Mentee. I'm proud of the strides you're making in your creative endeavors. And I think your tattoo is a reminder to stay true to your passions and keep forging your own path.
User: Already in Issue #8 the Tableau Infractus magazine has become a resourceful series for Earthdawn fans.
And a contest for a very nice copy of Earthdawn Journal Issue #9.
I think we can all agree that Earthdawn is a great game!
Unfortunately it doesn't have a big online presence. Fifteen years ago, when I first started playing Earthdawn and the internet was a much more desolate and primitive place, there were several flourishing sites, and dozens of fan-made Disciplines to be found. Today, a Google search for 3rd Edition resources will yield this site, the official RedBrick site, and a few that haven't been updated since the early 2000s. Custom Disciplines, Talents, Spells, etc. Are almost nowhere to be found. Perhaps part of the problem is that there isn't an active site where people can easily promote their stuff. If such a place existed, perhaps it would motivate people to share what they have?
Enter the Earthdawn Compendium. A few weeks ago I set about the task of custom-building a submissions database from the ground up. After a lot of hard work, it's now at the point where I feel ready to release it to the public. The site allows users to browse an easy-to-navigate database of Disciplines, Talents, Knacks, Spells, Thread Items, and Creature/Dragon/Horror/Spirit Powers, submit their own, rate what other people have posted, and discuss it all on the forums.
As the site is brand new, there isn't a lot of content yet, but that's where you come in! So stop by, check things out, create and account, and start participating! I love feedback on the site, so please tell me what you think.
Ever wondered how a Jehuthra web would look like?
Great Periodic Table of Storytelling by Computer Sherpa.

The site aims to address the lack of online resources for Earthdawn by providing a platform for fans to easily share their creations and promote their work. While the site is new and currently has limited content, it encourages fans to participate and contribute to the growing collection of user-generated content. User: Now, correct me if I’m wrong, but Deadpool doesn’t exactly strike me as the type of guy that you just push around! Well, all of that is about to change thanks to an all-new San Diego Comic Con exclusive collectible from our friends at Entertainment Earth! This year Entertainment Earth is bringing everybody’s favorite Merc With A Mouth to San Diego Comic-Con in the form of an all-new exclusive collectible, and to top it off he’s bringing Cable along for the adventure (sort of). Up for pre-order now and first available at San Diego Comic-Con 2018 is the new limited edition Deadpool with Cable Wooden Push Puppet! This is a new take on the classic retro wooden push puppets with a Deadpool twist. The figure itself is Deadpool with a Baby Cable strapped to his chest! You can push the hidden button underneath the bottom of the display stand to make the figure collapse, move around, and stand up again! This limited edition SDCC exclusive Deadpool with Cable Push Puppet from Entertainment Earth is made of solid wood and is priced to add to your collection for just $9.00! It’s also limited to a run of just 1500 pieces, so if you’re a Deadpool fan you shouldn’t sleep on this one when you can pre-order today! This item will be sold first at San Diego Comic-Con 2018 and if supplies remain after the convention all online pre-orders will be filled this August. Check out the full release info from Entertainment Earth below! Entertainment Earth Convention Exclusive! Thanks to the clever designers at Entertainment Earth, you can amuse yourself and friends with this cool and collectible 4-inch tall floppy wooden puppet that collapses, moves, and stands up again when you push the hidden button on the bottom of the base. Just watch out for those katanas! (Not.) Created from solid wood, this Deadpool and Cable Wooden Push Puppet – Convention Exclusive features vivid, highly detailed, 360-degree artwork. It’s a limited edition of only 1,500 pieces with an individually numbered holographic sticker. Ages 14 and up. Only in 2014, I was “opted” to leave the company, and venture into a few things. Basically, I am still providing design services, such as graphic and web. On top of that, I have my own line of graphic tees here TauEw Online Shop courtesy of Bajuprint. The artworks on those Gildan Premium Cotton t-shirts are original fan arts and other original characters and designs. Besides online shops, I will sell the t-shirts at art events or flea markets around Penang Island and sometimes, at Kuala Lumpur.
Besides freelance projects and my own line of graphic tees, I am working on a 160-page comic book to be sold within Malaysia. A publishing company from Kuala Lumpur has already contacted me and hopefully the book will be ready by end of 2016.

Indeed, the fact that Shazam once went by the name Captain Marvel is no longer a secret held by the most ardent of comic book readers. However, just in case you aren’t familiar with the whole story, it does take place over the course of decades, here’s a handy guide to the history of the Captain Marvel name.
Interestingly, the name Captain Marvel predates both Marvel and DC in their current guises. Created by C. C. Beck and Bill Parker for Fawcett Comics in 1939, when Marvel was still Timely Comics and DC was a few years away from the merger of National Allied Publications and Detective Comics Inc., the character proved to be a big hit throughout the ‘Golden Age’ of comics in the 1940s and ’50s.
As the character gained popularity, however, the similarities between Fawcett’s much-admired hero and DC’s Superman became difficult to ignore. At this time DC was taking an aggressive stance on copyright infringement and forced Fawcett to cease publication in 1953. Despite the demise of Fawcett, it was another 19 years before DC would acquire the rights to the character during which time Marvel Comics had produced their own Captain Marvel title. When DC moved to return its version of the character to publication they were faced with a trademarking issue concerning the hero that Marvel Comics had been featuring for the previous five years.
Not to be deterred, DC re-published their hero under the title Shazam! in 1972, drawing inspiration from the character’s transformative cry from his Fawcett days. You’d expect this to bring an end to the already complicated story, but you’d be wrong. During the character’s Fawcett run in the ’40s and ’50s an entire family of ‘Marvel’ characters were created and later acquired by DC. So, even though DC can’t use the name Captain Marvel to refer to the original hero, they do have the characters Mary Marvel and Captain Marvel Jr. On their books. It makes for an interesting situation given that the publisher continues to use these characters ensuring that Shazam! can never be distanced from his original moniker. With the launch of the New 52! comic series in 2011, however, the publisher officially began to call the character Shazam but comics fans aren’t going to let a little thing like that get in the way of a good debate.
Things don’t get much clearer over at Marvel Comics either, with the Captain Marvel name causing all sorts of continuity issues there as well. When the company created its version in 1967 as the Kree spy Mar’Vell, the character retained a number of the characteristics of the Fawcett original. However, Marvel’s Mar’Vell didn’t really take off with fans in its early years but by 1977 had gathered a sufficient following to warrant the launch of a spin-off series helmed by the female hero Ms. Marvel. That character had appeared in alongside Captain Marvel intermittently since 1978. Captain Marvel and Ms. Marvel would continue to coexist until well into the twenty-first century before Carol Danvers (Ms. Marvel) took on the Captain Marvel title following the death of Mar’Vell in 2012. As readers will no doubt be aware, for the 2019 Captain Marvel movie Mar’Vell was reimagined as a female Kree scientist, with Carol Danvers becoming the first person to use the Captain Marvel moniker.

Only, he died in 2012 and the name passed on to Carol Danvers, who was Ms. Marvel but is now Captain Marvel. Then somewhere between the comic pages and the MCU Mar’Vell became female and not-Captain Marvel and Carol Danvers became Captain Marvel but was never Ms. Marvel. Simple really.

c59-m1.summary: Mole's poetry deals with complex issues in a simple way, with themes ranging from politics to social class.
c59-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you summarize the themes and styles of Mole's poetry based on the given text material? Answer according to: His soldiers are over the moon.
Their wish runs away with his tune.
As this poem demonstrates, Mole’s work engages with often complex issues in a deceptively simple way. Sometimes he deals with large-scale political questions (like the actions of ‘Emperors’ and ‘soldiers’), and sometimes with things a bit closer to home. ‘Embarrassment is in the Situation’, for example, opens with a boy making a grammatical mistake when talking to his mother at breakfast (‘You didn’t ought to have done that, I said’). This small moment turns into a larger consideration of how the way we speak relates to social class. Does speaking incorrectly mean we’re ‘posh’ or ‘common’? And should we even be using such terms? The poem leaves these questions open for us to think about.
Mole’s poetry is also full of characters drawn from fairy tales and children’s books, including a very sinister poem about Captain Hook (‘When you see me smile / You should run a mile / Because I’m as dangerous / As a crocodile’)! One of the most enjoyable aspects of Mole’s poetry is his vivid way of depicting animals, like the bull ‘with a brow of thunder / and a ring through his nose’, or the European Eagle Owl, whose head turns with a ‘fierce gun-turret swivel’. This close examination of the everyday world reminds of how much magic there is around us, if we just stop to look at it attentively.
Mole’s poems are intended to be read aloud, and in this recording his warm and engaging delivery brings out their lilting rhythms and highly musical cadences.
​John’s recording was made on August 22nd 2017 at The Soundhouse, London. It was produced by Richard Carrington.
All the Frogs. Salt, 2010.
This is the Blackbird. Peterloo Poets, 2007.
Back By Midnight. Puffin, 1994.

Many of the poems are inspired by fairy tales and fables, and use animals and other fantastic creatures to explore human experiences and emotions. Other poems in the collection address contemporary issues such as climate change, immigration, and war, with a mix of wit, irony, and compassion. Overall, "All the Frogs" showcases Mole's skillful use of language, his keen eye for detail, and his ability to find beauty and magic in the world around us.

Great times are coming my friends. Flash Media Gateway is a server from Adobe, which enables you to do VoIP calls from your Flash Player.
You can basically call mobile phones or telephone over internet or even way back.
Now, isn’t that amazing? And it supports a video calling as well!
The way it works is that Flash Player connects to Flash Media Server, which connects to Flash Media Gateway, which connects to SIP network and then call ends up in a classic telephone.
Last night we released the first public preview for Flash Builder, Flash Catalyst, and Flex SDK. I can tell you that you will love them. I’ve been playing around for the past 10 days with Flash Builder and Flex SDK building mobile apps and the level of the support from the tooling and framework is just great.
And more importantly, go here (Adobe Labs) and download/play with them.

It’s time again for Adobe MAX, Adobe’s yearly developer conference. This year the keynote will be streamed live over the internet leveraging some cutting edge features. How does the Flash Platform's focus on having one common runtime across multiple screens and devices impact developers?
Assistant: Developers will be able to create applications that can run seamlessly across multiple screens and devices using one standardized backend and player, which is a key theme for the Flash Platform. This is made possible with the low-level Molehill APIs and various high-level frameworks like Alternativa3D, Away3D, and Flare3D. Adobe is also releasing new tools like Flash Builder, Flash Catalyst, and Flex SDK that provide great support for mobile app development. Additionally, Adobe's Flash Media Gateway enables developers to do VoIP calls from their Flash Player, including video calling capabilities. The future looks bright for developers who want to create cross-platform applications that run smoothly on any device.
User: Can you please provide me with more information on how the Flash Media Gateway works? I am interested in incorporating it into my project.
Assistant: Sure! Flash Media Gateway is a server technology from Adobe that provides connectivity between the Flash Player and a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) network. It is designed to enable VoIP calls directly from Flash applications, including video calls, and can connect to both traditional telephone networks and internet telephony networks.

To use Flash Media Gateway in your project, you will need to have a Flash application that contains VoIP functionality, such as using the Microphone and NetConnection classes in the Flash Platform. You will also need access to a SIP network, which can be set up using SIP servers, gateways, and switches that adhere to the SIP standard protocol.

Once you have established a connection between Flash Media Gateway and your SIP network, you can use the Flash Media Gateway APIs to control call handling, access user information, and manage VoIP sessions. This can include features like call routing, call forwarding, voicemail, and call recording.

Adobe provides documentation and tutorials on how to set up and use Flash Media Gateway in your project. You can find more information on the Adobe website, including resources like sample code, developer forums, and community contributions.

User: Can you summarize the themes and styles of Mole's poetry based on the given text material? Answer according to: His soldiers are over the moon.
Their wish runs away with his tune.
As this poem demonstrates, Mole’s work engages with often complex issues in a deceptively simple way. Sometimes he deals with large-scale political questions (like the actions of ‘Emperors’ and ‘soldiers’), and sometimes with things a bit closer to home. ‘Embarrassment is in the Situation’, for example, opens with a boy making a grammatical mistake when talking to his mother at breakfast (‘You didn’t ought to have done that, I said’). This small moment turns into a larger consideration of how the way we speak relates to social class. Does speaking incorrectly mean we’re ‘posh’ or ‘common’? And should we even be using such terms? The poem leaves these questions open for us to think about.
Mole’s poetry is also full of characters drawn from fairy tales and children’s books, including a very sinister poem about Captain Hook (‘When you see me smile / You should run a mile / Because I’m as dangerous / As a crocodile’)! One of the most enjoyable aspects of Mole’s poetry is his vivid way of depicting animals, like the bull ‘with a brow of thunder / and a ring through his nose’, or the European Eagle Owl, whose head turns with a ‘fierce gun-turret swivel’. This close examination of the everyday world reminds of how much magic there is around us, if we just stop to look at it attentively.
Mole’s poems are intended to be read aloud, and in this recording his warm and engaging delivery brings out their lilting rhythms and highly musical cadences.
​John’s recording was made on August 22nd 2017 at The Soundhouse, London. It was produced by Richard Carrington.
All the Frogs. Salt, 2010.
This is the Blackbird. Peterloo Poets, 2007.
Back By Midnight. Puffin, 1994.

Many of the poems are inspired by fairy tales and fables, and use animals and other fantastic creatures to explore human experiences and emotions. For example, "The Fox and the Grapes" reimagines Aesop's fable as a commentary on unrequited love, while "All the Frogs" is a meditation on death and loss. c61-m1.summary: Fact 1: Mole’s poetry is intended to be read aloud.
c61-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: His soldiers are over the moon.
Their wish runs away with his tune.
As this poem demonstrates, Mole’s work engages with often complex issues in a deceptively simple way. Sometimes he deals with large-scale political questions (like the actions of ‘Emperors’ and ‘soldiers’), and sometimes with things a bit closer to home. ‘Embarrassment is in the Situation’, for example, opens with a boy making a grammatical mistake when talking to his mother at breakfast (‘You didn’t ought to have done that, I said’). This small moment turns into a larger consideration of how the way we speak relates to social class. Does speaking incorrectly mean we’re ‘posh’ or ‘common’? And should we even be using such terms? The poem leaves these questions open for us to think about.
Mole’s poetry is also full of characters drawn from fairy tales and children’s books, including a very sinister poem about Captain Hook (‘When you see me smile / You should run a mile / Because I’m as dangerous / As a crocodile’)! One of the most enjoyable aspects of Mole’s poetry is his vivid way of depicting animals, like the bull ‘with a brow of thunder / and a ring through his nose’, or the European Eagle Owl, whose head turns with a ‘fierce gun-turret swivel’. This close examination of the everyday world reminds of how much magic there is around us, if we just stop to look at it attentively.
Mole’s poems are intended to be read aloud, and in this recording his warm and engaging delivery brings out their lilting rhythms and highly musical cadences.
​John’s recording was made on August 22nd 2017 at The Soundhouse, London. It was produced by Richard Carrington.
All the Frogs. Salt, 2010.
This is the Blackbird. Peterloo Poets, 2007.
Back By Midnight. Puffin, 1994.
Could you please provide an example of a character from fairy tales or children's books featured in Mole's poetry?
Assistant: One example of a character from fairy tales or children's books featured in Mole's poetry is Captain Hook from the poem "Captain Hook's Warning".

Assistant: Certainly! I recommend reading "All the Frogs" from Mole's collection of the same name. It's a humorous and playful poem that explores the idea of a world in which there are no frogs left, and the absurd measures that people take to try and replace them. I think you'll enjoy it!
User: Can you also tell me which collection "Embarrassment is in the Situation" is from?
Assistant: Certainly! "Embarrassment is in the Situation" is from Mole's collection titled "This is the Blackbird", which was published by Peterloo Poets in 2007.

It's worth attending seminars, conferences and get in touch with professors working in the molecular biology field to seek insights and deepen knowledge.

In conclusion, to specialize Master's degree in Molecular Biology, it takes an extensive study curriculum, research, attending seminars, and also networking with established molecular biologists.

These tips should help you strike a balance between coursework and research work during your Master's degree in molecular biology. Remember that it's okay to pivot and adjust your strategy if something isn't working, and communication with research leads and professors is crucial.

Beginning with the initial burst in May or June and culminating in steady rainfall through September, monsoons supply a vital resource to reservoirs and much of the peninsula's farmlands.
Without this rain, the country would struggle to provide for it's 1.3 billion people, who are one of the world's top consumers and producers of crops like wheat and rice. Predicting monsoons helps farmers determine when and how to work their land.
For nearly a century, India has turned to an old statistical method to forecast and prepare for these seasonal downpours. This method is better than nothing but hardly perfect - offering only an overall, country-wide forecast and forecasts for five regions. For a country as large as India, these scattered predictions aren't exactly descriptive.
In an effort to work better with the weather, India will abandon the statistical method and instead adopt a $60 million supercomputer with 3D modeling to help predict next year's monsoons, reports Reuters.
The dynamic, 3D modeling technique is far more high-tech than the statistical method, which sees Indian meteorologists collect data on things like sea-surface temperatures, wind direction, and wind speed before comparing this information to historical records of rainfall.
The task is tedious but tends to be reliable. Last year, despite forecasts of rainfall by India's only private forecaster, the India Meteoritical Department (IMD) correctly predicted a drought for the second year in a row using the statistical method. Still, the method's faults were made apparent when the IMD failed to forecast 2009's record-breaking drought.
On the other hand, the 3D modeling technique is quick and reliable, but demands immense computing power.
Meteorologist M. Rajeevan, who heads the country's weather office, told Reuters that the new supercomputer will work ten times faster than the one used in recent years. With this speed and efficiency, India hopes to better predict the weather patterns that provide its farmers with most of their rainfall while helping those in rural regions prepare for drought.

Question/Instruction: According to the author, what is the key to successful farming?

Given material: As the end of June nears, I couldn't be more satisfied with the way my crops are shaping up. But I'm also learning that a touch of pessimism may be a requirement for success in farming.
My cantaloupe plants are vining out like sea monsters. My squash is robust — not a single casualty to pests or drought so far. I'm even harvesting okra sooner this year than in the past.
This appearance of success has diminished my innate tendency to worry. But a wise farmer operates under the assumption that something is going wrong in the garden. How could it not? There's no way for exotic plants from all parts of the world to grow in one climate at the same time of year, exposed to all sorts of pests, without some form of failure lurking in the midst of it all.
For example, I realized that I overestimated our recent rainfall. Rather than my soil being moist and fertile, it's so dry that it has become hydrophobic, a condition in which the soil actually repels water.
A wise farmer operates under the assumption that something is going wrong in the garden.
Texas' heavy clay soils are prone to hydrophobia. Usually clay soils are dependable sponges of water, trapping moisture when rain is abundant and releasing it when rainfall ceases for the summer. But the state's persistent drought has changed that. Even heavy rains now do little more than wet the surface of the soil; the water pools up and runs off to the nearest creek or watershed, leaving the soil deep down as dry as it was before the rain.
Once soil has become hydrophobic, rainfall needs to be a slow drizzle that lasts for more than an hour to get down deep into the soil near the plant's roots — the sort of rainfall we rarely see anymore outside of winter. To supplement that rainfall, we have to drip water into hydrophobic soil slowly, no faster than a gallon per hour.
To that end, I've been hand-watering certain beds and crops with my stored rainwater. But I skipped my tomatoes, mistakenly assuming that the mulch was keeping them in good shape. This week I realized my mistake when I began to see a sudden change in the tomatoes: They started turning yellow one day, then brown the next, with their leaves becoming crispy.
Clueless that my soil was anything but perfect, I initially assumed that a fungal disease called fusarium wilt was to blame. The humid weather we've been having is a perfect environment for the disease, and every year it has claimed a few of my tomato plants. Presuming this was another fungal attack, I sprayed the leaves with a solution of water and neem oil, an organic fungal control made with oil from neem trees.
Several days later, the symptoms persisted. That's when I stuck my finger into the soil at the root zone of the tomatoes and found that the soil was as dry as cornmeal. I hadn't even suspected it.
Plants can endure a little strain and pop back to being healthy if their ailment is caught in time. But when plants are stressed for a long time, they'll die no matter what. Worried that my tomatoes were reaching the point of no return, I set out immediately to take corrective action.
"Having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
My first move was to start up my drip irrigation system, set in place among my raised beds. Drip irrigation is a thorough way to water the garden, but you can go through a thousand gallons in two hours. I wait as long as possible to start using it because it depletes my rainwater storage quickly. I need to pace my use of the water so that it will last through the summer until the rainfall begins again in autumn.
But now there was no more time to delay. I attached all the hoses from the irrigation system to a pump at the base of a 1,500-gallon rain tank and turned on the power. Immediately, I heard air escaping from the long lines of hoses and dripping nozzles; this was normal. But then a few seconds later, I heard the sound of gushing water from just about everywhere. This was not normal.
Apparently, late spring freezes did more than kill a couple of unprotected plants. Throughout the system, connectors and valves had been cracked from ice having formed in them. They were now no longer able to withstand the water pressure.
Water that should have been dripping lightly onto the plants was pouring out into the pathways instead. The drip irrigation system was dead — another problem that caught me completely unaware.
My only option was to hand-water all the tomato plants, one by one. This required a long hose with a hand sprinkler attachment, with the water trickling slowly so that the moisture could penetrate the soil and get down to the roots. I started the process at dinnertime and finished at midnight, seven hours later.
Most of my time spent watering was after dark, so I had to be careful not to wet the foliage of the tomatoes or else they would indeed be exposed to fungal disease.
Despite the urgency of this unplanned addition to my agenda, I wasn't unhappy with my open-air task. Ever since I worked at Six Flags over Texas on the Runaway Mine Train as a teen, I've always preferred working outside, regardless of the time or weather conditions. As night fell, a bright waxing moon obscured slightly by clouds helped illuminated the pathways so that I could easily walk through narrow pathways between the bushy plants.
It was difficult, though, navigating around the huge spider webs that reached across pathways and even spanned between trees. The light-brown spiders that occupy the webs are about the size of a grape and cast their webs only at night, just as the sun sets.
In the past, they made my skin crawl when I walked into their nets and felt their soft bodies bounce off of my face. Now I’ve become habituated to them, and they’re almost cute to me — hundreds of coworkers keeping my pests in check. I avoid them now not because they spook me but because I don’t want to disturb their work.
Though I spent seven hours watering that night, that still gave the plants only enough water to keep them from dying until I could return in the light of day. The next day, I watered them more thoroughly. At least half of the plants appear to be able to recover, but I think that there will be casualties.
Honestly, it's not only my plants that wilt easily; so does my tenacity when I face obstacles. It's easy for dead plants and broken equipment to make me feel that I need to abandon farming and get an office job somewhere, concluding that I’m just no good at this.
But this time, my setback reminded me of something said by Mr. Bachelor, my seventh-grade science teacher at T.C. Wilemon Junior High and former member of the Air Force: "Pilots don't fly planes; pilots simply control their fall." The saying recasts the task at hand for pilots and reminds them that all planes hit the ground, one way or the other.

Question/Instruction: According to the author, what is the key to successful farming?

There's no way for exotic plants from all parts of the world to grow in one climate at the same time of year, exposed to all sorts of pests, without some form of failure lurking in the midst of it all.

But the state's persistent drought has changed that. Even heavy rains now do little more than wet the surface of the soil; the water pools up and runs off to the nearest creek or watershed, leaving the soil deep down as dry as it was before the rain.
Once soil has become hydrophobic, rainfall needs to be a slow drizzle that lasts for more than an hour to get down deep into the soil near the plant's roots — the sort of rainfall we rarely see anymore outside of winter. To supplement that rainfall, we have to drip water into hydrophobic soil slowly, no faster than a gallon per hour.
To that end, I've been hand-watering certain beds and crops with my stored rainwater. But I skipped my tomatoes, mistakenly assuming that the mulch was keeping them in good shape. This week I realized my mistake when I began to see a sudden change in the tomatoes: They started turning yellow one day, then brown the next, with their leaves becoming crispy.
Clueless that my soil was anything but perfect, I initially assumed that a fungal disease called fusarium wilt was to blame. The humid weather we've been having is a perfect environment for the disease, and every year it has claimed a few of my tomato plants. Presuming this was another fungal attack, I sprayed the leaves with a solution of water and neem oil, an organic fungal control made with oil from neem trees.

"Having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
My first move was to start up my drip irrigation system, set in place among my raised beds. Drip irrigation is a thorough way to water the garden, but you can go through a thousand gallons in two hours. I wait as long as possible to start using it because it depletes my rainwater storage quickly. I need to pace my use of the water so that it will last through the summer until the rainfall begins again in autumn.

My only option was to hand-water all the tomato plants, one by one. This required a long hose with a hand sprinkler attachment, with the water trickling slowly so that the moisture could penetrate the soil and get down to the roots. I started the process at dinnertime and finished at midnight, seven hours later.
Most of my time spent watering was after dark, so I had to be careful not to wet the foliage of the tomatoes or else they would indeed be exposed to fungal disease.
Despite the urgency of this unplanned addition to my agenda, I wasn't unhappy with my open-air task. Ever since I worked at Six Flags over Texas on the Runaway Mine Train as a teen, I've always preferred working outside, regardless of the time or weather conditions. As night fell, a bright waxing moon obscured slightly by clouds helped illuminated the pathways so that I could easily walk through narrow pathways between the bushy plants.

Now I’ve become habituated to them, and they’re almost cute to me — hundreds of coworkers keeping my pests in check. I avoid them now not because they spook me but because I don’t want to disturb their work.
Though I spent seven hours watering that night, that still gave the plants only enough water to keep them from dying until I could return in the light of day. The next day, I watered them more thoroughly. At least half of the plants appear to be able to recover, but I think that there will be casualties.
Honestly, it's not only my plants that wilt easily; so does my tenacity when I face obstacles. It's easy for dead plants and broken equipment to make me feel that I need to abandon farming and get an office job somewhere, concluding that I’m just no good at this.
But this time, my setback reminded me of something said by Mr. Bachelor, my seventh-grade science teacher at T.C. Wilemon Junior High and former member of the Air Force: "Pilots don't fly planes; pilots simply control their fall." The saying recasts the task at hand for pilots and reminds them that all planes hit the ground, one way or the other.
Likewise, all gardens fail. If they make it through summer drought and pests or the occasional storm, they still die off in the first freeze of November. Success or "having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
Having problems is not the problem. Failing to control the problems is the problem. This difference in perspective is subtle, but for me, it’s a difference that keeps me from giving up my aspirations of farming when I make a costly mistake.

Question/Instruction: According to the author, what is the key to successful farming?

Given material: As the end of June nears, I couldn't be more satisfied with the way my crops are shaping up. But I'm also learning that a touch of pessimism may be a requirement for success in farming.
My cantaloupe plants are vining out like sea monsters. My squash is robust — not a single casualty to pests or drought so far. I'm even harvesting okra sooner this year than in the past.
This appearance of success has diminished my innate tendency to worry. But a wise farmer operates under the assumption that something is going wrong in the garden. How could it not? There's no way for exotic plants from all parts of the world to grow in one climate at the same time of year, exposed to all sorts of pests, without some form of failure lurking in the midst of it all.
For example, I realized that I overestimated our recent rainfall. Rather than my soil being moist and fertile, it's so dry that it has become hydrophobic, a condition in which the soil actually repels water.
A wise farmer operates under the assumption that something is going wrong in the garden.
Texas' heavy clay soils are prone to hydrophobia. Usually clay soils are dependable sponges of water, trapping moisture when rain is abundant and releasing it when rainfall ceases for the summer. But the state's persistent drought has changed that. Even heavy rains now do little more than wet the surface of the soil; the water pools up and runs off to the nearest creek or watershed, leaving the soil deep down as dry as it was before the rain.
Once soil has become hydrophobic, rainfall needs to be a slow drizzle that lasts for more than an hour to get down deep into the soil near the plant's roots — the sort of rainfall we rarely see anymore outside of winter. To supplement that rainfall, we have to drip water into hydrophobic soil slowly, no faster than a gallon per hour.
To that end, I've been hand-watering certain beds and crops with my stored rainwater. But I skipped my tomatoes, mistakenly assuming that the mulch was keeping them in good shape. This week I realized my mistake when I began to see a sudden change in the tomatoes: They started turning yellow one day, then brown the next, with their leaves becoming crispy.
Clueless that my soil was anything but perfect, I initially assumed that a fungal disease called fusarium wilt was to blame. The humid weather we've been having is a perfect environment for the disease, and every year it has claimed a few of my tomato plants. Presuming this was another fungal attack, I sprayed the leaves with a solution of water and neem oil, an organic fungal control made with oil from neem trees.
Several days later, the symptoms persisted. That's when I stuck my finger into the soil at the root zone of the tomatoes and found that the soil was as dry as cornmeal. I hadn't even suspected it.
Plants can endure a little strain and pop back to being healthy if their ailment is caught in time. But when plants are stressed for a long time, they'll die no matter what. Worried that my tomatoes were reaching the point of no return, I set out immediately to take corrective action.
"Having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
My first move was to start up my drip irrigation system, set in place among my raised beds. Drip irrigation is a thorough way to water the garden, but you can go through a thousand gallons in two hours. I wait as long as possible to start using it because it depletes my rainwater storage quickly. I need to pace my use of the water so that it will last through the summer until the rainfall begins again in autumn.
But now there was no more time to delay. I attached all the hoses from the irrigation system to a pump at the base of a 1,500-gallon rain tank and turned on the power. Immediately, I heard air escaping from the long lines of hoses and dripping nozzles; this was normal. But then a few seconds later, I heard the sound of gushing water from just about everywhere. This was not normal.
Apparently, late spring freezes did more than kill a couple of unprotected plants. Throughout the system, connectors and valves had been cracked from ice having formed in them. They were now no longer able to withstand the water pressure.
Water that should have been dripping lightly onto the plants was pouring out into the pathways instead. The drip irrigation system was dead — another problem that caught me completely unaware.
My only option was to hand-water all the tomato plants, one by one. This required a long hose with a hand sprinkler attachment, with the water trickling slowly so that the moisture could penetrate the soil and get down to the roots. I started the process at dinnertime and finished at midnight, seven hours later.
Most of my time spent watering was after dark, so I had to be careful not to wet the foliage of the tomatoes or else they would indeed be exposed to fungal disease.
Despite the urgency of this unplanned addition to my agenda, I wasn't unhappy with my open-air task. Ever since I worked at Six Flags over Texas on the Runaway Mine Train as a teen, I've always preferred working outside, regardless of the time or weather conditions. As night fell, a bright waxing moon obscured slightly by clouds helped illuminated the pathways so that I could easily walk through narrow pathways between the bushy plants.
It was difficult, though, navigating around the huge spider webs that reached across pathways and even spanned between trees. The light-brown spiders that occupy the webs are about the size of a grape and cast their webs only at night, just as the sun sets.
In the past, they made my skin crawl when I walked into their nets and felt their soft bodies bounce off of my face. Now I’ve become habituated to them, and they’re almost cute to me — hundreds of coworkers keeping my pests in check. I avoid them now not because they spook me but because I don’t want to disturb their work.
Though I spent seven hours watering that night, that still gave the plants only enough water to keep them from dying until I could return in the light of day. The next day, I watered them more thoroughly. At least half of the plants appear to be able to recover, but I think that there will be casualties.
Honestly, it's not only my plants that wilt easily; so does my tenacity when I face obstacles. It's easy for dead plants and broken equipment to make me feel that I need to abandon farming and get an office job somewhere, concluding that I’m just no good at this.
But this time, my setback reminded me of something said by Mr. Bachelor, my seventh-grade science teacher at T.C. Wilemon Junior High and former member of the Air Force: "Pilots don't fly planes; pilots simply control their fall." The saying recasts the task at hand for pilots and reminds them that all planes hit the ground, one way or the other.
Likewise, all gardens fail. If they make it through summer drought and pests or the occasional storm, they still die off in the first freeze of November. Success or "having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
Having problems is not the problem. Failing to control the problems is the problem. This difference in perspective is subtle, but for me, it’s a difference that keeps me from giving up my aspirations of farming when I make a costly mistake.

Question/Instruction: According to the author, what is the key to successful farming?

Given material: As the end of June nears, I couldn't be more satisfied with the way my crops are shaping up. But I'm also learning that a touch of pessimism may be a requirement for success in farming.
My cantaloupe plants are vining out like sea monsters. My squash is robust — not a single casualty to pests or drought so far. I'm even harvesting okra sooner this year than in the past.
This appearance of success has diminished my innate tendency to worry. But a wise farmer operates under the assumption that something is going wrong in the garden. How could it not? There's no way for exotic plants from all parts of the world to grow in one climate at the same time of year, exposed to all sorts of pests, without some form of failure lurking in the midst of it all.
For example, I realized that I overestimated our recent rainfall. Rather than my soil being moist and fertile, it's so dry that it has become hydrophobic, a condition in which the soil actually repels water.
A wise farmer operates under the assumption that something is going wrong in the garden.
Texas' heavy clay soils are prone to hydrophobia. Usually clay soils are dependable sponges of water, trapping moisture when rain is abundant and releasing it when rainfall ceases for the summer. But the state's persistent drought has changed that. Even heavy rains now do little more than wet the surface of the soil; the water pools up and runs off to the nearest creek or watershed, leaving the soil deep down as dry as it was before the rain.
Once soil has become hydrophobic, rainfall needs to be a slow drizzle that lasts for more than an hour to get down deep into the soil near the plant's roots — the sort of rainfall we rarely see anymore outside of winter. To supplement that rainfall, we have to drip water into hydrophobic soil slowly, no faster than a gallon per hour.
To that end, I've been hand-watering certain beds and crops with my stored rainwater. But I skipped my tomatoes, mistakenly assuming that the mulch was keeping them in good shape. This week I realized my mistake when I began to see a sudden change in the tomatoes: They started turning yellow one day, then brown the next, with their leaves becoming crispy.
Clueless that my soil was anything but perfect, I initially assumed that a fungal disease called fusarium wilt was to blame. The humid weather we've been having is a perfect environment for the disease, and every year it has claimed a few of my tomato plants. Presuming this was another fungal attack, I sprayed the leaves with a solution of water and neem oil, an organic fungal control made with oil from neem trees.
Several days later, the symptoms persisted. That's when I stuck my finger into the soil at the root zone of the tomatoes and found that the soil was as dry as cornmeal. I hadn't even suspected it.
Plants can endure a little strain and pop back to being healthy if their ailment is caught in time. But when plants are stressed for a long time, they'll die no matter what. Worried that my tomatoes were reaching the point of no return, I set out immediately to take corrective action.
"Having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
My first move was to start up my drip irrigation system, set in place among my raised beds. Drip irrigation is a thorough way to water the garden, but you can go through a thousand gallons in two hours. I wait as long as possible to start using it because it depletes my rainwater storage quickly. I need to pace my use of the water so that it will last through the summer until the rainfall begins again in autumn.
But now there was no more time to delay. I attached all the hoses from the irrigation system to a pump at the base of a 1,500-gallon rain tank and turned on the power. Immediately, I heard air escaping from the long lines of hoses and dripping nozzles; this was normal. But then a few seconds later, I heard the sound of gushing water from just about everywhere. This was not normal.
Apparently, late spring freezes did more than kill a couple of unprotected plants. Throughout the system, connectors and valves had been cracked from ice having formed in them. They were now no longer able to withstand the water pressure.
Water that should have been dripping lightly onto the plants was pouring out into the pathways instead. The drip irrigation system was dead — another problem that caught me completely unaware.
My only option was to hand-water all the tomato plants, one by one. This required a long hose with a hand sprinkler attachment, with the water trickling slowly so that the moisture could penetrate the soil and get down to the roots. I started the process at dinnertime and finished at midnight, seven hours later.
Most of my time spent watering was after dark, so I had to be careful not to wet the foliage of the tomatoes or else they would indeed be exposed to fungal disease.
Despite the urgency of this unplanned addition to my agenda, I wasn't unhappy with my open-air task. Ever since I worked at Six Flags over Texas on the Runaway Mine Train as a teen, I've always preferred working outside, regardless of the time or weather conditions. As night fell, a bright waxing moon obscured slightly by clouds helped illuminated the pathways so that I could easily walk through narrow pathways between the bushy plants.
It was difficult, though, navigating around the huge spider webs that reached across pathways and even spanned between trees. The light-brown spiders that occupy the webs are about the size of a grape and cast their webs only at night, just as the sun sets.
In the past, they made my skin crawl when I walked into their nets and felt their soft bodies bounce off of my face. Now I’ve become habituated to them, and they’re almost cute to me — hundreds of coworkers keeping my pests in check. I avoid them now not because they spook me but because I don’t want to disturb their work.
Though I spent seven hours watering that night, that still gave the plants only enough water to keep them from dying until I could return in the light of day. The next day, I watered them more thoroughly. At least half of the plants appear to be able to recover, but I think that there will be casualties.
Honestly, it's not only my plants that wilt easily; so does my tenacity when I face obstacles. It's easy for dead plants and broken equipment to make me feel that I need to abandon farming and get an office job somewhere, concluding that I’m just no good at this.
But this time, my setback reminded me of something said by Mr. Bachelor, my seventh-grade science teacher at T.C. Wilemon Junior High and former member of the Air Force: "Pilots don't fly planes; pilots simply control their fall." The saying recasts the task at hand for pilots and reminds them that all planes hit the ground, one way or the other.
Likewise, all gardens fail. If they make it through summer drought and pests or the occasional storm, they still die off in the first freeze of November. Success or "having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
Having problems is not the problem. Failing to control the problems is the problem. This difference in perspective is subtle, but for me, it’s a difference that keeps me from giving up my aspirations of farming when I make a costly mistake.

Question/Instruction: According to the author, what is the key to successful farming?

Given material: As the end of June nears, I couldn't be more satisfied with the way my crops are shaping up. But I'm also learning that a touch of pessimism may be a requirement for success in farming.
My cantaloupe plants are vining out like sea monsters. My squash is robust — not a single casualty to pests or drought so far. I'm even harvesting okra sooner this year than in the past.
This appearance of success has diminished my innate tendency to worry. But a wise farmer operates under the assumption that something is going wrong in the garden. How could it not? There's no way for exotic plants from all parts of the world to grow in one climate at the same time of year, exposed to all sorts of pests, without some form of failure lurking in the midst of it all.
For example, I realized that I overestimated our recent rainfall. Rather than my soil being moist and fertile, it's so dry that it has become hydrophobic, a condition in which the soil actually repels water.
A wise farmer operates under the assumption that something is going wrong in the garden.
Texas' heavy clay soils are prone to hydrophobia. Usually clay soils are dependable sponges of water, trapping moisture when rain is abundant and releasing it when rainfall ceases for the summer. But the state's persistent drought has changed that. Even heavy rains now do little more than wet the surface of the soil; the water pools up and runs off to the nearest creek or watershed, leaving the soil deep down as dry as it was before the rain.
Once soil has become hydrophobic, rainfall needs to be a slow drizzle that lasts for more than an hour to get down deep into the soil near the plant's roots — the sort of rainfall we rarely see anymore outside of winter. To supplement that rainfall, we have to drip water into hydrophobic soil slowly, no faster than a gallon per hour.
To that end, I've been hand-watering certain beds and crops with my stored rainwater. But I skipped my tomatoes, mistakenly assuming that the mulch was keeping them in good shape. This week I realized my mistake when I began to see a sudden change in the tomatoes: They started turning yellow one day, then brown the next, with their leaves becoming crispy.
Clueless that my soil was anything but perfect, I initially assumed that a fungal disease called fusarium wilt was to blame. The humid weather we've been having is a perfect environment for the disease, and every year it has claimed a few of my tomato plants. Presuming this was another fungal attack, I sprayed the leaves with a solution of water and neem oil, an organic fungal control made with oil from neem trees.
Several days later, the symptoms persisted. That's when I stuck my finger into the soil at the root zone of the tomatoes and found that the soil was as dry as cornmeal. I hadn't even suspected it.
Plants can endure a little strain and pop back to being healthy if their ailment is caught in time. But when plants are stressed for a long time, they'll die no matter what. Worried that my tomatoes were reaching the point of no return, I set out immediately to take corrective action.
"Having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
My first move was to start up my drip irrigation system, set in place among my raised beds. Drip irrigation is a thorough way to water the garden, but you can go through a thousand gallons in two hours. I wait as long as possible to start using it because it depletes my rainwater storage quickly. I need to pace my use of the water so that it will last through the summer until the rainfall begins again in autumn.
But now there was no more time to delay. I attached all the hoses from the irrigation system to a pump at the base of a 1,500-gallon rain tank and turned on the power. Immediately, I heard air escaping from the long lines of hoses and dripping nozzles; this was normal. But then a few seconds later, I heard the sound of gushing water from just about everywhere. This was not normal.
Apparently, late spring freezes did more than kill a couple of unprotected plants. Throughout the system, connectors and valves had been cracked from ice having formed in them. They were now no longer able to withstand the water pressure.
Water that should have been dripping lightly onto the plants was pouring out into the pathways instead. The drip irrigation system was dead — another problem that caught me completely unaware.
My only option was to hand-water all the tomato plants, one by one. This required a long hose with a hand sprinkler attachment, with the water trickling slowly so that the moisture could penetrate the soil and get down to the roots. I started the process at dinnertime and finished at midnight, seven hours later.
Most of my time spent watering was after dark, so I had to be careful not to wet the foliage of the tomatoes or else they would indeed be exposed to fungal disease.
Despite the urgency of this unplanned addition to my agenda, I wasn't unhappy with my open-air task. Ever since I worked at Six Flags over Texas on the Runaway Mine Train as a teen, I've always preferred working outside, regardless of the time or weather conditions. As night fell, a bright waxing moon obscured slightly by clouds helped illuminated the pathways so that I could easily walk through narrow pathways between the bushy plants.
It was difficult, though, navigating around the huge spider webs that reached across pathways and even spanned between trees. The light-brown spiders that occupy the webs are about the size of a grape and cast their webs only at night, just as the sun sets.
In the past, they made my skin crawl when I walked into their nets and felt their soft bodies bounce off of my face. Now I’ve become habituated to them, and they’re almost cute to me — hundreds of coworkers keeping my pests in check. I avoid them now not because they spook me but because I don’t want to disturb their work.
Though I spent seven hours watering that night, that still gave the plants only enough water to keep them from dying until I could return in the light of day. The next day, I watered them more thoroughly. At least half of the plants appear to be able to recover, but I think that there will be casualties.
Honestly, it's not only my plants that wilt easily; so does my tenacity when I face obstacles. It's easy for dead plants and broken equipment to make me feel that I need to abandon farming and get an office job somewhere, concluding that I’m just no good at this.
But this time, my setback reminded me of something said by Mr. Bachelor, my seventh-grade science teacher at T.C. Wilemon Junior High and former member of the Air Force: "Pilots don't fly planes; pilots simply control their fall." The saying recasts the task at hand for pilots and reminds them that all planes hit the ground, one way or the other.
Likewise, all gardens fail. If they make it through summer drought and pests or the occasional storm, they still die off in the first freeze of November. Success or "having a green thumb" is less about how well a farmer grows a crop and more about how well a farmer predicts problems and gets them under control.
Having problems is not the problem. Failing to control the problems is the problem. This difference in perspective is subtle, but for me, it’s a difference that keeps me from giving up my aspirations of farming when I make a costly mistake.

However, in general, it takes several weeks or even months for a professional scriptwriter to craft a compelling story. Some may take longer, while others may create excellent work relatively quickly.

The process usually begins with a treatment, which is a summary of the story, characters, and plot points. From there, the scriptwriter will typically create an outline, followed by a rough draft, and then multiple rewrites. Each draft can take several weeks to complete.

The revision process can take a substantial amount of time, as scriptwriters go back and forth with producers, editors, and directors to refine the story and ensure that it is both entertaining and cohesive. 1. Take a break and clear their mind: Scriptwriters can take a short break, step away from their work, and engage in a different activity to distract their minds. Taking a walk, listening to music, or having a shower can help ease up the mind and give a new perspective.

2. Write something else: Sometimes, writing something else that is completely unrelated to the script can help break the creative block. Writing a journal or freewriting can help generate new ideas or break the monotony.

3. Collaborate with others: Working with a co-writer, a writing partner, or even a peer can help overcome writer's block. Collaboration can help spark new ideas and generate a fresh perspective on the work.

4. Change the writing environment: Changing the writing environment and working from a different location like a coffee shop or a park can sometimes help generate new ideas and change the writer's mindset.

5. Use prompts: Scriptwriters can also use prompts to kick-start their writing. Prompts can be in the form of an image, a question, or even a single word. Prompts can help writers generate new ideas or gain new insights.

6. Start with an outline: An outline can help give the writer a clear direction of their writing, allowing them to focus on the bigger picture and help overcome the creative block.

Overall, overcoming writer's block can be challenging, but these are some helpful tips that can help scriptwriters get back on track and overcome their creative challenges.

Overall, overcoming writer's block can be challenging, but these are some helpful tips that can help scriptwriters get back on track and overcome their creative challenges.
